title: Small state, strong farming presence
finding: Agriculture makes up 9.1% of Tasmania’s businesses, versus 4.9% in NSW.
note: Colour shows a share of actively trading businesses, not land area or employment. Main-state allocation; class-cell sums are approximate.

title: New South Wales has the most businesses
finding: New South Wales has 45,163 agricultural businesses; Tasmania has 4,015.
note: Smaller circles reduce crowding; their area remains proportional to business count. Points represent state totals, not farm locations. Unknown/other geography is excluded from maps.

title: Fewer registered dairy farms
finding: Registered dairy farms fell 44.3%, from 6,770 to 3,772.
note: This is a dairy-only series, not a count of all farms. The financial year runs July–June; 2024–25 is provisional.

title: Every state has fewer farming businesses
finding: South Australia fell 2.3%; Queensland was almost unchanged (−0.1%).
note: Open circles are the June 2024 baseline (0%). Diamonds show the change to June 2025. Original counts remain in the tooltips and table. Small differences, especially in territories, may reflect confidentiality adjustments.

title: Victoria accounts for most of the decline
finding: Victoria accounts for 508 of the 648 fewer registered dairy farms.
note: Floating bars subtract each state’s contribution. This is an accounting comparison, not an explanation of why farms left. End year provisional.

title: Farmers are concentrated in older age groups
finding: An estimated 59% of Farmers and Farm Managers are aged 55+.
note: Teal males on the left; ochre females on the right. The centre line marks zero. Values are survey estimates in thousands. “Farmer” is an occupation, not everyone working in agriculture. Source sex categories are retained.

title: Business staffing differs between states
finding: Dairy’s non-employing share spans about 48–78% across eligible states.
note: Pale boxes hold the middle half of state shares; the dark line is the median. Larger dots show individual states, offset vertically for visibility; only horizontal position represents percentage. Each state counts equally. Include ≥100 businesses and ≥5 eligible states per sector. Owners and family may still work.

title: Where each sector stands out
finding: Dairy makes up a larger business share in Victoria and Tasmania than across the eight states combined.
note: Each cell divides a sector’s share within that state by its share across all eight states. Darker blue means greater concentration. Below 1× is under-represented; above 1× is over-represented. This compares business mix, not productivity or absolute counts. Labels highlight dairy in Victoria and Tasmania; choose a sector for its labels. Exact values are in tooltips and the table. Small territory counts can produce volatile ratios.

title: Business size depends on the sector
finding: About 60% of poultry businesses report annual turnover of at least AUD 200,000.
note: Each bar totals 100%. Rows rank the share with annual sales of at least 2 million Australian dollars. Sales are not profit. Labels include the smaller high-sales shares; narrow segments use outside labels. Three bands combine six published bins; confidentiality adjustments can affect totals.

title: Victoria is the centre of dairy farming
kicker: GEOGRAPHY AND FARM COUNTS, SIDE BY SIDE
finding: Victoria holds 65.6% of Australia’s registered dairy farms.
note: Left: complete geographic reference, including NT and ACT. Right: six reported state silhouettes, resized with a common area-per-farm scale and arranged in rows for comparison. Shape area represents farms, not land. NT and ACT counts are not reported; they are not zeros.

title: Most businesses have no employees
finding: About 75.6% of the derived agriculture-business total is non-employing.
note: The outlined group contains businesses with employees, divided by staff count. Area counts businesses, not workers. Owners and family may still work without employees. Blue shows businesses without employees; gold shows businesses with employees. Leader lines name all four staff-size groups, including the smallest. Bin sum 144,678, versus published-class total sum 144,681: the difference reflects confidentiality adjustments.

title: A smaller agricultural workforce
finding: The annual average fell from 375,000 in 2000 to 247,000 in 2025.
note: One point per complete year; the vertical axis starts at zero. The latest quarter is separate: about 245,900 workers in February 2026. This counts the agriculture industry, not just the farmer occupation.
